Velocity and recoil

The box often shows the shot velocity, in metres per second or feet per second (fps). For clay cartridges it is usually about 360–430 m/s (roughly 1,200–1,400 fps).

Compare velocities with care. Shot slows down quickly after it leaves the barrel, so it matters where the speed is measured. European makers (following the C.I.P. test rules) usually measure 2.5 m from the muzzle and write 'V2.5'; some write 'V1', measured at 1 m, which gives a higher number. Labels are not always consistent, so treat the figure as a rough guide.

American makers give feet per second measured about 3 ft (0.9 m) from the muzzle. British boxes sometimes quote an estimated muzzle velocity. So the same figure does not necessarily mean the same speed.

A faster cartridge slightly shortens the time the shot takes to reach the target, but it kicks harder, and its pattern is not necessarily better. Many coaches suggest not chasing speed but choosing a cartridge you shoot consistently with and that does not tire you.

Recoil is the push of the gun into the shoulder when it fires. It grows with a heavier load and a higher velocity, and it falls with a heavier gun. A gas-operated semi-automatic spreads the push over a longer time, so many shooters feel it as softer.

Gun fit and a correct gun mount matter even more. A gun that fits you and sits firmly in the shoulder feels much softer than one resting on the arm or on bone. A good butt pad and a steady stance help too. More: Gun fit basics and Recoil, shoulder and neck.

Tip: In a day of Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ or Compak® Sporting you may fire 100–200 shots. Heavy recoil tires you and can slowly teach you to flinch before the shot. So a lighter cartridge in practice, 24 g for example, is a sensible choice, not a weakness.

Key points

  • Typical clay cartridge velocity: about 360–430 m/s (roughly 1,200–1,400 fps).
  • Makers measure velocity differently (V1, V2.5, fps).
  • Faster means more recoil, but not necessarily better results.
  • Recoil grows with load and velocity and falls with gun weight.
  • Good fit and a correct mount reduce felt recoil.

Did you know?

Shot reaches a target at 30 m in roughly a tenth of a second. In that time a crossing target can move a metre or two, which is why shooters give it lead.

Check yourself · 3 questions

  1. What makes recoil weaker?

    1. A heavier load
    2. A higher velocity
    3. A heavier gun
    4. A stock that is too short
    Answer

    A heavier gun

    A heavier gun absorbs the push better; a heavier load and a higher velocity increase recoil.

  2. Why should you not compare velocities from different makers directly?

    1. Makers measure them in different ways
    2. The box figure is usually invented
    3. All cartridges have the same velocity
    4. Velocity has no effect at all
    Answer

    Makers measure them in different ways

    V1, V2.5 and fps at 3 ft are different measurements, so the same figure does not mean the same cartridge.

  3. What is a typical velocity for clay cartridges?

    1. About 100 m/s
    2. About 360–430 m/s
    3. About 900 m/s
    4. Over 1,500 m/s
    Answer

    About 360–430 m/s

    Most clay cartridges are about 360–430 m/s.
